questions.question: Explain why some volcanic eruptions are gentle while others are violently explosive, and link each eruption style to the type of volcano it builds.
questions.expected_answer: The controlling property is viscosity, which depends mainly on silica content. Magma low in silica is basaltic: it is very hot, around 1 100 to 1 200 degrees Celsius, and so runny that dissolved gases escape freely as it rises. Pressure therefore never builds, and eruptions are effusive — lava pours out and flows a long way before solidifying, building a shield volcano that is very wide with slopes of only a few degrees, such as Mauna Loa or Marion Island. Magma high in silica is andesitic or rhyolitic: it is cooler and thick enough to plug its own vent, so gas is trapped and pressure builds behind the plug until the volcano is blown apart. These explosive eruptions eject pyroclastic material — ash, cinders and bombs — and where explosive and effusive phases alternate, the ash layers and lava layers stack into a tall, steep-sided composite volcano such as Fuji or Vesuvius. Where only fragments are thrown out, a small steep cinder cone forms; where the lava is too viscous to flow at all, it piles into a dome.

questions.question: Distinguish between extrusive and intrusive volcanic landforms, and explain, using South African examples, how intrusive features become visible landforms.
questions.expected_answer: Extrusive landforms are built by material that reached the surface: cones, craters, calderas, lava flows, lava plateaux, hot springs and geysers. The Drakensberg and the Lesotho highlands are a lava plateau, built about 180 million years ago when Gondwana began to break apart and very fluid basalt poured from long fissures in sheet after sheet, which is why the skyline is a wall of flat-topped stepped ramparts rather than peaks. Intrusive landforms form where magma cools and solidifies underground: batholiths (large granite masses, exposed at Paarl Rock), lopoliths (saucer-shaped, the Bushveld Igneous Complex being the largest on earth and the source of the world's greatest platinum and chromium reserves), laccoliths (dome-shaped, arching the strata above), sills (sheets forced horizontally between existing layers) and dykes (sheets cutting vertically across them). Intrusive features become landforms only through differential erosion: Karoo dolerite is far harder than the shale around it, so an exposed sill caps a hill and protects it, producing the region's characteristic flat-topped koppies on an eroded plain, while an exposed dyke weathers into a long straight wall of rock. A volcanic neck is magma solidified in the pipe itself, left standing when the softer cone erodes away; the kimberlite pipes at Kimberley and Cullinan are pipes of this kind that brought diamonds up from the mantle.

questions.question: Volcanic areas are among the most dangerous places on earth, yet millions choose to live on them. Discuss the hazards and the benefits, and describe how volcanic risk is managed.
questions.expected_answer: The hazards are severe. Lava flows destroy property but seldom kill because most move slowly; the true killer is the pyroclastic flow, an avalanche of superheated gas, ash and rock that races downslope faster than anyone can escape. Ash falls collapse roofs, smother crops and pasture, contaminate water, damage lungs and ground aircraft; lahars, volcanic mudflows formed when ash mixes with rain or melted snow, follow valleys and bury settlements far from the volcano; and poisonous gases, landslides, tsunamis and short-term global cooling after very large eruptions add to the list. The benefits explain why people stay: weathered volcanic ash and lava make exceptionally fertile soils rich in potassium, phosphorus and magnesium, supporting dense farming populations in Java, Sicily and the Ethiopian highlands; geothermal energy heats Iceland and supplies a large share of Kenya's electricity; volcanic settings concentrate minerals, including Bushveld platinum and chromium and the diamonds of the kimberlite pipes; and volcanic rock, hot springs and dramatic scenery support construction and tourism. Management succeeds better than for earthquakes because rising magma gives warning: monitoring tracks earthquake swarms, ground swelling on tiltmeters and satellites, increased gas emission and rising ground temperature, and feeds graded alert levels. Hazard maps show which valleys lahars will follow and which slopes lie in the path of pyroclastic flows; planning keeps permanent settlement out of the worst zones and fixes evacuation routes and shelters in advance; and community education ensures that when the alert is raised, people move in hours rather than days.
